stem: A 48-year-old woman comes to the office due to intermittent ear discharge over the last 2 years.  She has also noticed decreased hearing in the right ear recently.  Medical history is significant for obesity, hyperlipidemia, seasonal allergies, and diet-controlled diabetes mellitus.  Otoscopy shows a small perforation in the right tympanic membrane and a pearly mass behind the membrane.  Conductive hearing loss is noted in the right ear.  The remainder of the ear, nose, and throat examination is normal.  Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's aural mass?​‌​‌​‌​​‌​​‌​​​​‌​​​‌​​​​​‌‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌​​​​‌‌​​​​​​​‌‌‌​​​​‌​‌​‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​​​​​​‌​​​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌​​​​​‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​​‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌​‌​​​​​​‌‌​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌​​​‌​​​​‌​​‌​​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​​​​​‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌‌​​​‌‌​​‌​​​​​​​‌‌​​‌‌​​​​​‌‌​​​‌‌‌​‌​​‌​‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌​​​‌‌‌​​
explanation:
This patient has findings consistent with a cholesteatoma, an abnormal growth within the middle ear that can occur congenitally or be acquired (more common) due to recurrent infections/effusions, trauma, or surgery involving the middle ear.

Pathogenesis of acquired cholesteatoma involves entry of keratinizing squamous epithelium from the external surface of the tympanic membrane (TM) into the middle ear, which is normally lined by respiratory epithelium (eg, simple cuboidal/columnar, often ciliated).  Continued desquamation then leads to progressive trapping and accumulation of keratin debris.  Acquired cholesteatomas most commonly develop by one of the following mechanisms:

  • Tympanic membrane perforation, usually due to acute otitis media (AOM) or iatrogenic injury (eg, tympanostomy tube placement).  The discontinuity allows squamous epithelium to migrate into the middle ear.  Ongoing keratin shedding produces a pearly white mass behind the TM, and a visible perforation is often present (as in this patient).

  • Eustachian tube dysfunction causing chronic negative middle-ear pressure, which is commonly associated with recurrent AOM or chronic effusion.  The persistent negative pressure pulls the TM inward (usually the pars flaccida), forming retraction pockets (invaginations) that extend into the middle ear that gradually accumulate white, keratinaceous debris.

The most common manifestation of a cholesteatoma is persistent, painless otorrhea due to chronic inflammation/infection of the keratin debris.  Cholesteatomas can also produce lytic enzymes that erode nearby structures such as the auditory ossicles, which can result in conductive hearing loss, as seen in this patient.  Less commonly, erosion into the vestibular apparatus or facial nerve can cause vertigo or facial palsies, respectively.

(Choice A)  Otomycosis, or fungal infection of the external auditory canal, can present with ear discharge but also classically causes pain and deep-seated itching.  In addition, a mass posterior to the TM would not be seen.

(Choice B)  A facial nerve neuroma can grow in the middle ear because the facial nerve courses through this territory.  Although conductive hearing loss can occur, unilateral facial paralysis would be expected and is not seen in this patient.  In addition, chronic otorrhea and TM perforation would not be expected.

(Choice C)  Squamous cell carcinoma is the most common malignant tumor of the ear canal.  It typically presents as an ulcerated plaque or nodule, and otorrhea and hearing loss can occur.  Unlike in this patient, the external auditory canal is typically erythematous, edematous, and friable.

(Choice D)  Granulomatous disease of the middle ear is uncommon and usually develops with systemic disease, such as sarcoidosis or granulomatosis with polyangiitis.

Educational objective:Cholesteatomas are collections of keratin debris and squamous epithelium within the middle ear.  Common presenting symptoms include chronic, painless otorrhea and conductive hearing loss; a pearly white mass may be visible behind the tympanic membrane.​‌​‌​‌​​‌​​‌​​​​‌​​​‌​​​​​‌‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌​​​​‌‌​​​​​​​‌‌‌​​​​‌​‌​‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​​​​​​‌​​​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌​​​​​‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​​‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌​‌​​​​​​‌‌​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌​​​‌​​​​‌​​‌​​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​​​​​‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌‌​​​‌‌​​‌​​​​​​​‌‌​​‌‌​​​​​‌‌​​​‌‌‌​‌​​‌​‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌​​​‌‌‌​​
